entities.summary:
Guitmund (died 1084), a Benedictine monk and later Bishop of Aversa in Norman Southern Italy, emerged as a principal theological adversary of Berengar of Tours during the intense 11th-century Eucharistic controversies. His rigorous defense of the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist positioned him at the forefront of orthodox Latin theology, directly influencing papal policy and shaping the intellectual landscape of the nascent Gregorian Reform. Guitmund's contributions were crucial in articulating and solidifying the doctrine that would later be termed transubstantiation, at a time when the nature of the sacrament was fiercely debated.

Originally a monk at the Abbey of La Croix-Saint-Leufroy in Normandy, Guitmund was renowned for his sharp intellect and unwavering adherence to traditional doctrine. He authored *De corporis et sanguinis Christi veritate in Eucharistia*, a seminal treatise likely composed between 1075 and 1077, which systematically refuted Berengar's symbolic interpretation of the Eucharist. This work became a standard text for anti-Berengarian polemicists, meticulously outlining the arguments for the substantial change of the elements. His theological acumen earned him recognition from Pope Gregory VII, who appointed him as a cardinal-priest before elevating him to the Bishopric of Aversa in 1077 or 1078, thereby extending his influence into the political and ecclesiastical landscape of Southern Italy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Guitmund's rigorous theological work decisively shaped the Latin Church's doctrine of the Eucharist, providing a foundational argument for transubstantiation that influenced centuries of Catholic theology and was formally adopted at the Fourth Lateran Council.
